analysis.one_liner: Lets states and the FCC cap cable TV rates and enforce service standards where cable faces no competition.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee for 18 months without a hearing or vote; in July 1992 the record points to a broader cable bill, H.R. 4850, as the vehicle that went forward, and Congress passed cable rate regulation that year over a presidential veto.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1986, federal law had barred most state and local scrutiny of cable rates, and cable prices rose far faster than inflation while most customers had no competing provider to turn to. This bill would let states, certified by the FCC, regulate cable rates in areas without effective competition, and would set national standards for customer service, signal quality, billing, and complaint handling. It would also require cable systems to carry local broadcast stations and bar cable-owned program channels from discriminating against rival distributors.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers — about 59% of TV households at the time — who faced a local monopoly provider. They would get rate regulation where no effective competition exists, minimum technical and customer-service standards, clearer billing and complaint procedures, guaranteed carriage of local broadcast stations, and a ban on cable-owned programmers discriminating against competing distributors.

how_it_helps.text: States certified by the FCC could regulate cable rates (including fees, charges, and deposits) wherever a cable system lacks effective competition, defined as less than 30% local subscription or two unaffiliated providers each reaching 80% of households; the FCC would regulate rates where no certified state does [S2][S3].

The bill responds to GAO findings that between 1986 and 1989 the lowest-priced cable service rose 43.1% and the most popular service rose 39.4%, versus roughly 12% CPI growth, and that 97% of franchises were exempt from any direct rate scrutiny [S3].

The FCC would have to set customer service standards covering office hours, installation and repair response times, billing and refunds, price disclosure, and complaint resolution, while states and cities could impose stricter standards [S2][S3].
Cable operators would have to carry local independent and public broadcast stations as a condition of keeping their copyright license, protecting access to local news and diverse viewpoints [S2][S3].

Programmers in which a cable operator holds an interest could no longer unreasonably refuse to deal with, or discriminate in price and terms against, competing multichannel distributors — a key barrier to competition at the time [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, whose rates and fees would become subject to review in markets without competition, and cable-affiliated program networks, which would have to sell their channels to rival distributors on non-discriminatory terms. Operators would also bear annual financial disclosures and compliance with new technical and service standards.

drawbacks.text: Rate regulation of a capital-intensive monopoly can dull the incentive to invest in system upgrades; the bill itself instructs regulators to weigh operator profitability and allow a 'reasonable profit', acknowledging this trade-off [S3].
Must-carry rules consume cable channel capacity that could otherwise carry new programming services [S3].
The effective-competition test leaves systems above the threshold unregulated, so some subscribers in weakly competitive markets could still see little protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer case was strong: documented rate increases of roughly 40% against 12% inflation, with 97% of franchises exempt from any rate scrutiny, made the case that neither competition nor regulation was protecting subscribers. The main honest cost is that regulating a monopoly's rates can slow investment in better networks, and must-carry occupies channel space; the bill tried to soften both with profitability tests and state flexibility. On balance the consumer protections outweighed those costs, and a version of most of these ideas became law in 1992.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee in February 1991, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote; in July 1992 the record redirects further action to a separate cable bill, H.R. 4850, which became the Cable Act of 1992.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Shays (R-CT), joined by Reps. Pallone, Downey, and Wilson, introduced the bill on January 16, 1991 [S3][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on January 16, 1991, and to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance on February 11, 1991 [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history; on July 23, 1992 the record states 'For Further Action See H.R.4850', a broader cable bill taken up that year [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 without this bill ever reaching the House floor [S1].
Congress did enact cable rate regulation and consumer standards in 1992 through the successor cable legislation, which passed over President George H.W. Bush's veto.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators kept charging rates largely free of regulation through 1991 and most of 1992 while this bill sat in committee. Consumers ultimately gained most of the substance through the successor bill, which became the Cable Act of 1992 after Congress overrode the president's veto.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable operators, until the 1992 successor law

sides.party_line_note: A House Republican sponsored the bill and 12 of 267 House Democrats joined 1 Republican as cosponsors; no roll calls ever occurred because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would subject their rates, fees, equipment charges, and service practices to state or FCC review in markets without competition, ending the rate-setting freedom they had held since 1986. Their gain from unregulated monopoly pricing came directly out of subscribers' bills.

Program channels owned by cable companies could no longer refuse to deal with, or price-discriminate against, rival satellite and wireless distributors, which had been a major barrier to competition with cable itself.
Must-carry rules would guarantee local stations a place on cable systems, protecting their reach and the diversity of local programming available to subscribers.
The non-discrimination rules would give rival distributors access to cable-owned programming on similar terms, strengthening the competition the bill says was missing.
